title: Commitments and Spot: The Two Big Discounts
intro: On-demand is the most expensive way to buy compute. There are two large discounts: promise to keep spending for one or three years (Savings Plans, reservations, committed-use discounts), or take spare capacity that can be reclaimed at short notice (spot, preemptible). Each fits a different kind of workload. The queries cover September 2026.

steps.prompt: See how much of last month's eligible compute spend was covered by Savings Plans.
steps.explanation: 30% of compute spend got the discounted rate; 70%, $28,794, was billed at full on-demand prices.
steps.why: Coverage is the share of your usage that's discounted. Low coverage on a workload that runs steadily all year means paying a premium for flexibility you aren't using. There's no single right number: it depends on how stable your baseline is. Many teams aim to cover the level of usage they never drop below.

steps.prompt: Check the other side: of the commitment already bought, how much was actually used?
steps.explanation: 100% utilisation: every dollar committed was used.
steps.why: Coverage and utilisation pull against each other. Utilisation is whether the commitment you bought is being used; unused commitment is money paid for nothing. 100% utilisation with 30% coverage means the commitment is safe and too small: there's room to buy more. Low utilisation means you over-committed, perhaps because a service was shut down or moved after the purchase.

steps.prompt:
Which usage is a commitment the right fit for?
  a) A batch job that runs for one week a year
  b) The steady baseline that runs around the clock all year: the databases and the minimum number of servers
  c) A new experiment that may be cancelled next month
  d) Peak traffic on the busiest day
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
usage over a year:
  |        ___ peak (on-demand or spot)
  |   ____/   \____
  |__/_____________\__   variable (autoscaled on-demand, spot where it can be)
  |__________________   baseline: commit to this
steps.hint: You pay for a commitment whether you use it or not.
steps.explanation: Commit to the floor, not the ceiling.
steps.why: A commitment is a bet that usage stays at least this high for the term. The baseline is the safe bet. Compute Savings Plans are the flexible kind: they follow you across instance families, sizes, regions, and to Fargate and Lambda, so a later rightsizing or a move to ARM doesn't strand them. Instance-specific reservations are cheaper and rigid. Buy in small, staggered purchases so they don't all expire at once.

steps.prompt: Now spot. Look at recent spot prices for the instance type m7g.xlarge running Linux, the last 5 records.
steps.explanation: About 6 cents an hour, where on-demand is about 16: over 60% off.
steps.why: Spot is the cloud selling idle capacity cheaply, with one condition: it can take the instance back with two minutes' warning. Prices vary by instance type and zone, and so does how often capacity is reclaimed. The more instance types and zones a workload can accept, the cheaper and more stable it is, which is why Karpenter and spot fleets are given a list of types and choose among them.

steps.prompt:
Which workload should NOT run on spot?
  a) Stateless web servers behind a load balancer, with several replicas
  b) CI build agents
  c) A single primary database with no replica
  d) Batch jobs that checkpoint their progress
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
good on spot : stateless, replicated, restartable, or checkpointed work
bad on spot  : anything whose loss with two minutes' notice is an outage or loses data
steps.hint: What happens if the machine disappears in two minutes?
steps.explanation: A lone database can't tolerate a two-minute eviction.
steps.why: Spot fits work that can lose a node without anyone noticing. To use it well: handle the interruption notice (drain the node, finish or checkpoint the job), spread across zones and instance types, and keep a base of on-demand capacity under the spot layer. In Kubernetes this needs PodDisruptionBudgets and graceful shutdown to be right first, which is worth having anyway.
